subsection: 2. Calculating ΔH and the heat of neutralisation

notes.b: Neutralisation gives out heat, and that heat can be measured with a thermometer. This experiment turns a temperature rise into an enthalpy change (ΔH, the heat change of a reaction) for hydrochloric acid reacting with sodium hydroxide.
points: Aim: to determine the heat of neutralisation (ΔH) of hydrochloric acid by sodium hydroxide, using primary data (results you measure yourself in the experiment).
Heat of neutralisation is the heat change when one mole of water is formed in the reaction between an acid and a base, i.e. one mole of H⁺ ions reacting with one mole of OH⁻ ions.
Equation: HCl(aq) + NaOH(aq) → NaCl(aq) + H₂O(l); ionic equation (showing only the ions that actually react): H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l).
ΔH is the heat change at constant pressure. The cup is open to the atmosphere, so the pressure stays constant during the reaction.

The heat released by the reaction is absorbed by the solution, so the heat produced is found from the temperature rise of the solution: Q = m × c × ΔT (Q is the heat, m the mass of solution, c its specific heat capacity and ΔT the temperature rise).
notes.tip: You may be asked to define heat of reaction or heat of neutralisation, and to give evidence that the reaction is exothermic. Say the heat is per mole of water formed, and that the temperature of the solution rises.

notes.b: The method mixes equal amounts of acid and base in an insulated cup and records the highest temperature reached. Each step is there to give an accurate temperature rise.
points: Step 1: using a graduated cylinder (or, more accurately, a burette or pipette), measure 50.0 cm³ of 1.00 M hydrochloric acid into a polystyrene foam cup, which insulates the reaction.
Step 2: measure 50.0 cm³ of 1.00 M sodium hydroxide into a second cup or beaker, so the two solutions stay separate until mixed.
Step 3: allow both solutions to reach room temperature, then measure the temperature of each with a thermometer reading to 0.1 °C (or a temperature sensor).
Step 4: rinse and dry the thermometer between the two measurements so no solution is carried across. If the two temperatures differ, take their average as the initial temperature.
Step 5: add the sodium hydroxide to the acid quickly and all at once, put on the lid, and stir gently with the thermometer (or a stirrer).
Step 6: record the highest temperature reached, because the heat produced is worked out from the biggest rise.
Step 7: repeat the experiment and use the mean temperature rise, which reduces the effect of a single poor reading.
Diagram: a polystyrene cup with a lid, a thermometer through the lid into the solution, a stirrer, and the cup standing in a beaker for support.
notes.tip: Exams ask for the precautions needed to get an accurate maximum temperature, and how to get the initial temperature if the two solutions start at different temperatures. Take the average of the two readings.

notes.b: Every detail of the method has a reason, and the exam asks for these reasons. Most of them are about stopping heat escaping or making a small temperature change easier to read.
points: Polystyrene foam is a good insulator with a very low heat capacity, so little heat is lost to the surroundings or absorbed by the cup; glass or metal would conduct heat away and absorb heat.
The lid reduces heat loss by convection (heat carried away by moving air) and evaporation.

Moderately concentrated (1.00 M) solutions give a large enough temperature rise (about 7 °C) to measure accurately; with 0.1 M solutions the rise would be under 1 °C, and the percentage error in reading it would be very large.
Equal amounts of acid and base (same volume and concentration) are used so that all of each reacts, so the moles of water formed is known.
Mixing quickly and stirring make the reaction complete at once and spread the heat evenly, so the true maximum temperature is recorded before heat is lost.
A thermometer reading to 0.1 °C is needed because the temperature change is small.
A burette or pipette measures volumes more accurately than a graduated cylinder.
The disadvantage of adding the base slowly from a burette is that heat is lost while it is added.
notes.tip: Be ready to give the advantages of a polystyrene cup, why moderately concentrated solutions are used, and an advantage and a disadvantage of a burette compared with a graduated cylinder.

notes.b: In the simple method, the mixture starts cooling as soon as it reaches its peak, so the highest reading is a little too low. A temperature–time graph corrects for this.
points: Record the temperature of the acid every 30 s for a few minutes before mixing, then add the base at a recorded time.
Record the temperature every 30 s for several minutes after mixing, so the whole rise and the cooling that follows are captured.
After the maximum, the temperature falls gradually because heat is lost to the surroundings.

Plot temperature against time and extrapolate (extend) the cooling line back to the time of mixing. The temperature rise read from the graph allows for heat lost while the mixture was warming up, giving a more accurate ΔT.
Diagram: a temperature–time graph with a flat line before mixing, a sharp rise, a gently falling line after the maximum, and the falling line extended back to the time of mixing to give ΔT.
notes.tip: If asked why the temperature falls after the maximum, the answer is heat lost to the surroundings.

notes.b: To turn the temperature rise into ΔH, find the heat produced, then divide by the moles of water formed. Each step uses the total mass of the mixture, not the mass of acid alone.
points: Data: 50.0 cm³ of 1.00 M HCl and 50.0 cm³ of 1.00 M NaOH; initial temperature 18.4 °C; maximum 25.0 °C.
Temperature rise: ΔT = 25.0 − 18.4 = 6.6 °C = 6.6 K; a temperature change is the same in °C and K, so no conversion is needed.
Mass of solution: 100 cm³ × 1.00 g cm⁻³ = 100 g = 0.100 kg, assuming the density and specific heat capacity are those of water.
Heat produced: Q = m × c × ΔT = 0.100 kg × 4.18 kJ kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ × 6.6 K = 2.76 kJ.
Moles of water formed = moles of HCl = 1.00 × 0.0500 = 0.0500 mol.
Heat per mole: 2.76 kJ ÷ 0.0500 mol = 55.2 kJ mol⁻¹, because ΔH is defined per mole of water formed.
The reaction gives out heat, so ΔH = −55.2 kJ mol⁻¹: Q is the heat gained by the solution, and ΔH is the heat lost by the reaction.

Comparison: the accepted value for a strong acid with a strong base is about −57 kJ mol⁻¹; the experimental value is less negative mainly because some heat was lost to the surroundings and absorbed by the cup and thermometer.
notes.tip: Use the total mass of the mixture (100 g), not just the acid's 50 g. Do not add 273 to a temperature change. If c is given in J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ (4180), the answer comes out in J, so divide by 1000 for kJ. Give ΔH a negative sign.

notes.b: The result does not depend on which strong acid or base you use, but it does change for weak ones. Acids that release two H⁺ ions need extra care when counting moles.
points: All strong acid–strong base neutralisations have almost the same ΔH, about −57 kJ mol⁻¹, because the acids and bases are fully dissociated (split completely into ions) and the only reaction is H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l); the other ions are spectators.
With a weak acid (e.g. ethanoic acid) or a weak base (e.g. ammonia), ΔH is slightly less negative, because some energy is used to complete the dissociation of the weak acid or base as it reacts.
With a diprotic acid (one that can give two H⁺ ions per molecule), count moles of water, not moles of acid: H₂SO₄(aq) + 2NaOH(aq) → Na₂SO₄(aq) + 2H₂O(l).
Sample data: 25.0 cm³ of 2.00 M H₂SO₄ + 50.0 cm³ of 2.00 M NaOH, with ΔT = 17.8 K.
Moles of water = moles of NaOH = 2.00 × 0.0500 = 0.100 mol, so ΔH = −55.8 kJ mol⁻¹ per mole of water.
Doubling the volumes of the same solutions gives the same ΔT: twice the moles react and twice the heat is produced, but it heats twice the mass of solution.
notes.tip: Heat of neutralisation is per mole of water formed, not per mole of acid; this matters for H₂SO₄. For weak acids do not give exact values; say slightly less negative. Doubling or tripling the volumes gives the same ΔT, for the reason in the last point.

notes.b: The solutions are hazardous, and the experiment always gives a value that differs from the accepted one. Knowing which errors push the value which way lets you suggest improvements.
points: Safety: 1.00 M hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide are corrosive (they damage skin and eyes), sodium hydroxide especially to the eyes; wear safety glasses and gloves and wipe up spills.
Both bottles carry the GHS corrosion pictogram: liquid dripping from two test tubes onto a hand and a surface.

Errors that make the value less negative: heat lost to the air and bench; heat absorbed by the cup and thermometer; not recording the true maximum temperature; solutions starting at different temperatures.
Assumption error: the solution's density and specific heat capacity are taken as those of water.
Improvements: use the temperature–time graph, a lid, two nested cups, a more precise thermometer or temperature sensor, and burettes or pipettes for volumes.
notes.tip: You may be asked to identify the corrosive hazard pictogram, so know its description. The bomb calorimeter is not on the specification.

notes.b: An enthalpy change varies with the conditions it is measured in. So chemists agree one set of conditions, so that values from different reactions can be compared fairly.
points: Enthalpy changes depend on temperature, pressure and the physical states of the substances, so values are quoted under a standard set of conditions to allow comparison.
Standard conditions for enthalpy changes: a temperature of 25 °C (298 K) and a pressure of 1 atmosphere (101.3 kPa).
Solutions have a concentration of 1 mol L⁻¹, and each substance is in its standard state, its normal physical state under these conditions, e.g. water as a liquid and carbon as graphite.
A standard enthalpy change is written ΔH° (ΔH with a superscript ⦵ or °), so the symbol shows the value refers to standard conditions.
IUPAC (the international chemistry body) now uses 100 kPa (1 bar) as standard pressure; the difference from 101.3 kPa has a negligible effect on ΔH values.
Standard conditions are not s.t.p. (standard temperature and pressure: 0 °C, 273 K and 101.3 kPa), which is used for gas volumes. There is more on this in Molar volume and Avogadro's law.
notes.tip: You may be asked to state the standard conditions for enthalpy changes and why they are needed. Standard conditions (25 °C) are not s.t.p. (0 °C).

notes.b: Any reaction that happens in solution can have its ΔH found by the same five steps used in the neutralisation experiment. The idea is to use the temperature change of a known mass of water or solution to find the heat, then scale to one mole.
points: Step 1: carry out the reaction in an insulated container (a polystyrene cup) with a known mass of water or solution, and measure the temperature change, ΔT.
Step 2: calculate the heat transferred to the water or solution: Q = m × c × ΔT, where m is the mass of water or solution in kg and ΔT is the temperature change in K or °C.
Here c is the specific heat capacity of the water or solution, 4.18 kJ kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ for water.

Step 3: calculate the moles of the reactant that reacted completely (the limiting reactant, the one that runs out first), using n = concentration × V (in L) for solutions or n = m ÷ M for solids and liquids.
Step 4: heat per mole = Q ÷ n, in kJ mol⁻¹, scaled to the moles in the balanced equation if the heat of reaction is asked for.

Step 5: give ΔH a sign: negative if the temperature rose (exothermic, giving out heat), positive if it fell (endothermic, taking in heat). Q is always positive; the sign of ΔH comes only from whether the temperature rose or fell.
Specific heat capacity, c, is the heat needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1 K; for water it is 4.18 kJ kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ (= 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹).
Dilute solutions are assumed to have the same specific heat capacity as water and a density of 1.00 g cm⁻³, so 1 cm³ of solution is taken as 1 g.
If a heat capacity, C, of the whole mixture is given (in kJ K⁻¹ or J K⁻¹), use Q = C × ΔT instead.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to explain ΔH and to calculate the heat produced and ΔH from temperature data. Use the moles of the limiting reactant, not of the reactant in excess, and remember that a ΔT in K equals a ΔT in °C.

notes.h: Worked example: zinc and copper(II) sulfate (sample data)
notes.b: This displacement reaction (a more reactive metal pushing a less reactive one out of solution) is measured in the same way as neutralisation. The key extra step is choosing the limiting reactant.
points: Data: excess zinc powder was added to 50.0 cm³ of 0.200 M copper(II) sulfate solution in a polystyrene cup; the temperature rose by 10.0 °C.
Equation: Zn(s) + CuSO₄(aq) → ZnSO₄(aq) + Cu(s); ionic equation: Zn(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + Cu(s).
Zinc is in excess, so the copper(II) sulfate is the limiting reactant and fixes how much reacts.
Moles of CuSO₄ = 0.200 × 0.0500 = 0.0100 mol.
Heat per mole = 2.09 ÷ 0.0100 = 209 kJ mol⁻¹; the temperature rose, so ΔH = −209 kJ mol⁻¹.
The value is a little less negative than the accepted value because of heat losses. There is more on errors and improvements in Investigation: heat of neutralisation.
notes.tip: Use the moles of the limiting reactant (here copper(II) sulfate), not of the zinc in excess.

notes.h: Using ΔH to find heat for a given amount
notes.b: A ΔH value is a heat per mole, so once you know it you can predict the heat for any amount of reactant. Work out the moles, then multiply.
points: ΔH refers to the moles in the equation as written, so the heat for any amount is found by proportion.
Example: CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l), ΔH = −890 kJ mol⁻¹; M(CH₄) = 16 g mol⁻¹, so 8.0 g of methane is 8.0 ÷ 16 = 0.50 mol.
Burning 0.50 mol of methane releases 0.50 × 890 = 445 kJ, because half a mole gives half the heat of a full mole.
Example: 0.0500 mol of HCl neutralised released 2.86 kJ, so 1 mol would release 2.86 ÷ 0.0500 = 57.2 kJ and ΔH = −57.2 kJ mol⁻¹.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to calculate the heat that would be produced if 1 mole reacted.

notes.b: An energy profile diagram is a graph of how the energy of a reaction changes as it goes from reactants to products. It shows both the overall heat change and the energy barrier the reaction has to climb.
points: An energy profile diagram shows how the energy (enthalpy) of the reacting system changes during the reaction, with energy on the vertical axis and progress of reaction (reaction pathway) on the horizontal axis.
It shows the reactants' level, a hump rising to a maximum, and the products' level; unlike an enthalpy level diagram (which only compares the two levels), it shows this hump.
The height of the hump above the reactants is the activation energy (Ea), the minimum energy needed for a reaction to happen. There is more on this in Catalysis and energy profiles.
ΔH is the vertical difference between the reactants' and products' levels and does not depend on the height of the hump.
Exothermic profile: products below reactants, ΔH is negative, and the energy released as bonds form is greater than the activation energy taken in.
Endothermic profile: products above reactants, ΔH is positive, and the activation energy is larger than ΔH.

Energy transfer: the energy taken in to climb the hump goes into breaking bonds, and the energy given out on the way down comes from bond making; the net difference is transferred as heat to the surroundings (exothermic) or from them (endothermic).

Diagram: an exothermic profile and an endothermic profile, each with axes labelled, reactants and products named, Ea marked with an arrow from the reactants to the top of the hump, and ΔH marked with an arrow from reactants to products.
notes.tip: You may be asked to draw an energy profile for an exothermic reaction showing ΔH and the activation energy. An energy profile has a hump; an enthalpy level diagram does not. Calculating ΔH from bond enthalpies or heats of formation is Higher Level and belongs elsewhere.

keyTerms.definition: The heat change when one mole of water is formed in the reaction between an acid and a base.
The heat needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1 K.
An acid that is fully dissociated in water, such as hydrochloric acid.
An acid that is only partly dissociated in water, such as ethanoic acid.
An acid that can give two H⁺ ions per molecule, such as sulfuric acid.
An ion that appears unchanged on both sides of an ionic equation.
Extending a line on a graph beyond the plotted points to estimate a value, such as the temperature at the time of mixing.
A temperature of 25 °C (298 K) and a pressure of 1 atmosphere (101.3 kPa), used to quote enthalpy changes for comparison.
The normal physical state of a substance under standard conditions, such as water as a liquid.
An enthalpy change measured under standard conditions, with solutions at 1 mol L⁻¹.
The reactant that is used up first and so determines the amount of product and heat.
The minimum energy needed for a reaction to happen, shown as the height of the hump on an energy profile.
A graph of energy against progress of reaction showing the reactants, the activation energy, the products and ΔH.
The route of the reaction from reactants to products, shown on the horizontal axis of an energy profile.

questions.prompt: Describe how you would measure the heat of neutralisation of hydrochloric acid by sodium hydroxide, explaining the reasons for the container used and the precautions taken to obtain an accurate maximum temperature.
questions.model: Measure 50.0 cm³ of 1.00 M hydrochloric acid into a polystyrene foam cup, and 50.0 cm³ of 1.00 M sodium hydroxide into a second cup or beaker. Let both solutions reach room temperature, measure each temperature to 0.1 °C, and use the average as the initial temperature. Add the sodium hydroxide to the acid quickly and all at once, put on the lid and stir gently, then record the highest temperature reached. Repeat and use the mean temperature rise. Polystyrene foam is used because it is a good insulator with a very low heat capacity, so little heat is lost or absorbed by the cup. The lid reduces heat loss by convection and evaporation. Mixing quickly and stirring make the reaction complete at once and spread the heat evenly, so the true maximum is recorded before heat is lost. Moderately concentrated solutions are used so that the temperature rise is large enough, about 7 °C, to be measured accurately.

questions.prompt: 80 cm³ of 1.0 M hydrochloric acid was added to 80 cm³ of 1.0 M sodium hydroxide. The temperature rose by 6.7 °C. Taking the density of the solution as 1.0 g cm⁻³ and its specific heat capacity as 4.18 kJ kg⁻¹ K⁻¹, calculate (i) the moles of HCl, (ii) the heat produced, (iii) ΔH (sample data).
questions.model: (i) Moles of HCl = 1.0 mol L⁻¹ × 0.080 L = 0.0800 mol. (ii) Mass of solution = 160 cm³ × 1.0 g cm⁻³ = 160 g = 0.160 kg. Heat produced Q = 0.160 kg × 4.18 kJ kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ × 6.7 K = 4.48 kJ. (iii) Moles of water formed = moles of HCl = 0.0800 mol, so heat per mole = 4.48 kJ ÷ 0.0800 mol = 56.0 kJ mol⁻¹. The reaction gives out heat, so ΔH = −56.0 kJ mol⁻¹.

questions.prompt: Explain why the heat of neutralisation is almost the same for all strong acids with strong bases, and why the same temperature rise is obtained if the volumes of both solutions are doubled.
questions.model: For all strong acids with strong bases, the acids and bases are fully dissociated and the only reaction is H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l); the other ions are spectators, so ΔH is about −57 kJ mol⁻¹ in every case. If the volumes of both solutions are doubled, twice the moles of acid and base react, so twice the heat is produced. However, twice the mass of solution is heated by that heat, so the temperature rise is the same.

questions.prompt: Excess zinc was added to 100 cm³ of 0.100 M copper(II) sulfate solution and the temperature rose by 4.8 °C. Calculate ΔH for Zn + CuSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Cu, taking the specific heat capacity of the solution as 4.18 kJ kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ and its density as 1.00 g cm⁻³ (sample data).
questions.model: Mass of solution = 100 cm³ × 1.00 g cm⁻³ = 100 g = 0.100 kg. Heat produced Q = 0.100 kg × 4.18 kJ kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ × 4.8 K = 2.01 kJ. Moles of CuSO₄ = 0.100 mol L⁻¹ × 0.100 L = 0.0100 mol, and zinc is in excess, so CuSO₄ is the limiting reactant. Heat per mole = 2.01 kJ ÷ 0.0100 mol = 201 kJ mol⁻¹. The temperature rose, so ΔH = −201 kJ mol⁻¹.

questions.prompt: Draw a labelled energy profile diagram for an exothermic reaction, marking the activation energy and ΔH, and explain what the diagram shows about the energy transfer.
questions.model: Draw axes: energy on the vertical axis and progress of reaction on the horizontal axis. Draw a reactants level, a hump rising to a maximum, and a products level below the reactants level. Mark the activation energy Ea with an arrow from the reactants to the top of the hump, and mark ΔH with an arrow from the reactants level down to the products level. The energy taken in to climb the hump goes into breaking bonds, and the energy given out on the way down comes from bond making. The products are at lower energy, so the net energy difference is transferred as heat to the surroundings, and ΔH is negative. The energy released as bonds form is greater than the activation energy taken in.

questions.prompt: State the standard conditions for enthalpy changes and explain why they are needed.
questions.model: The standard conditions are a temperature of 25 °C (298 K), a pressure of 1 atmosphere (101.3 kPa), solutions at a concentration of 1 mol L⁻¹, and each substance in its standard state. They are needed because enthalpy changes depend on temperature, pressure and the physical states of the substances, so quoting values under the same conditions allows them to be compared.
